lesson_title: The Torn Newspaper: How We Know the Continents Move
hook_text: Same fossil in the Karoo and in Brazil. A reptile that could not swim. Explain that.
clip_script: Tear a page of the Sunday paper in half and give the halves to two people. Years later both pieces turn up. How do you prove they were once one page? Not by the ragged edge — you check whether the SENTENCES run across the tear. Same for the continents. The ragged edge is the coastline: South America slots into the bulge of Africa. But the proof is the sentences. Fossils: Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could no more swim the Atlantic than you could — its bones lie in the Karoo, and identical bones lie in Brazil. Rocks: stand in the Cape Fold Mountains near Worcester and you are in a range that carries on, same age, same squeeze, in Argentina and in Antarctica. Ice: at the base of the Karoo rocks is rubble dumped by a glacier — an ice sheet, in the Northern Cape — and the scratches it carved only make sense when you push the continents back together. Wegener said all of this in 1912 and was laughed at for one reason. He could not say what pushed.
visual_style: A torn newspaper page whose halves drift apart into the shapes of Africa and South America, fossil bones and mountain ranges glowing where the print lines up across the tear.
mood: Detective-story build, ending on an unresolved question.
pacing: Slow, deliberate setup with the paper; three quick evidence beats; a hard stop on the last line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to find out what pushes — and what happens where the plates meet.
